subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove by mathematical induction that 1² + 2² + 3² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.25, chapter 4 MATHEMATICAL INDUCTION, Short Answer question 1(ii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The split gives one mark to each of the four moves an induction proof is marked on — the base case, the hypothesis, the inductive step and the closing appeal to the principle — and leaves the opening statement step unmarked, matching every other card in this chapter. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, and Mathematical Induction supplies one of them on almost every paper. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, the five moves, and how the bracket factorises in the third step.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — the nth term and the full S(n) line are what Step 3 works on.

recall.must_convey: That the nth term is n² and S(n) is the full statement, the sum of squares up to n² equals n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
accept: the nth term is n squared and s of n says the sum of squares equals n into n plus one into two n plus one over six
general term n squared then write out s of n in full
each term is a square so the nth term is n squared
nth term n squared ani rasi s of n rastam

steps.why: The series is given as a pattern. Naming the nth term as n² is what lets you write the exact term to add to both sides in Step 3.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as 2n instead of n², which is the wrong series.
Leaving S(n) unwritten, so Step 3 has no line to work from.
steps.memory_tip: Three factors on the right: n, then n + 1, then 2n + 1, all over 6. The 2n + 1 is the odd one to remember.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Work out BOTH sides separately at n = 1 and say they are equal.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 1 times 2 times 3 over 6, which is also 1, so S(1) is true.
accept: left side is one squared which is one and right side is one two three over six which is one
put n equals one in both sides and both come to one
the first case gives one on each side
n equals one pettina rendu sides one vasthai

steps.why: Induction needs a true first case to start from. However good the inductive step is, without S(1) the chain has nothing to stand on.
common_mistakes: Asserting S(1) is true without working out both sides.
Putting n = 1 into 2n + 1 and getting 2 instead of 3.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1 the right side is 1 × 2 × 3 over 6, which is 6/6 = 1. Write both sides, then write that they are equal.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume it for ONE value k and number the line (1) — Step 3 quotes that number.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is assumed true for some k in N — the sum of squares up to k² equals k(k+1)(2k+1)/6 — and the line is numbered (1).
accept: assume it for k so the sum up to k squared equals k into k plus one into two k plus one over six
suppose s of k holds and call that equation one
take it as true for one value k in the naturals and number the line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: let it be true for k
then I assume s of k

steps.why: This is the assumption the method rests on. It is granted for one value only, and Step 3 has to earn the right to pass it on to the next value.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Replace every n by k, including inside 2n + 1, and number the line (1).

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Add (k+1)² to both sides of (1), take (k+1) out, then factorise the quadratic.
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That (k+1)² is added to both sides of (1), (k+1) comes out as a common factor, and 2k² + 7k + 6 factorises as (k+2)(2k+3), giving the formula with n replaced by k+1.
accept: add k plus one squared to both sides take k plus one out and the quadratic factorises into k plus two into two k plus three
put in the next term take the common factor out and you get k plus one into k plus two into two k plus three over six
two k squared plus seven k plus six splits into k plus two and two k plus three
next term add chesi common factor teeste k plus two into two k plus three vasthundi
reject: I show s of k plus one
heard_as: two k squared plus seven k plus six

steps.why: The added term (k+1)² shares the factor (k+1) with the assumed sum. Once that comes out, the quadratic left inside is 2k² + 7k + 6, which splits as (k+2)(2k+3) — exactly the two brackets the formula needs at k+1.
common_mistakes: Adding (k+1) instead of (k+1)² as the next term.
Expanding everything into a cubic instead of factorising, which will not simplify.
Writing the target as (k+1)(k+2)(2k+1) and forgetting that 2n + 1 becomes 2k + 3.
steps.memory_tip: Take (k+1) out first. What is left is 2k² + 7k + 6 = (k+2)(2k+3), and 2k + 3 is 2(k+1) + 1.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one full mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the result holds for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k gives s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for all n
hence by p m i the statement is true for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The earlier steps prove two single statements — one about n = 1 and one about a step. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and is worth a full mark on its own.
